newsitem.title: UK: Orangemen sweat it out on streets of Belfast.
newsitem.headline: Orangemen sweat it out on streets of Belfast.

text.p: Sweating in their elaborate uniforms, hundreds of bandsmen pounded out a deafening blast of drum and flute music as Northern Ireland's Protestant Orange Order marched through Belfast on Saturday.

The Orangemen cancelled contentious parades through Catholic areas where violence had been feared but they made up for it on their own turf as band after marching band poured through the centre of the Northern Ireland capital.
The "Loyal Orange Lodges" (branches) marched behind their ceremonial banners bearing images symbolic of their deep Protestant faith and loyalty to the British crown.

The pounding drums bore the names of the lodges, redolent of long devotion to the union with Britain. The forefathers of the Rising Sons of the Somme lodge were among thousands of Ulstermen who perished in the World War One battle in France.

Behind the bands came the more senior lodge members, solemn looking men in black bowler hats -- long out of fashion in mainland Britain -- with Orange sashes round their necks and elaborate armlets on their sleeves.
They carried the ceremonial swords and pikes of their order, while others bore the crown and the bible on velvet cushions.
Younger members looked more dishevelled, with their formal Orange sashes worn incongruously over casual shirts not tucked into their jeans.
As an estimated 80,000 Orangemen were on the march across Northern Ireland, thousands of families lined the parade routes from early in the morning, determined to have a good day out.

The parades on the "Glorious 12th of June" are the high point of the Orange Order's annual marching season, when they mark a Protestant victory over Catholic forces at the Battle of the Boyne in 1690.
The decision to reroute the parades away from nationalist flashpoints was not universally popular.
One angry Protestsnt man insisted the parade should have been allowed down Belfast's Catholic Lower Ormeau Road.
"It was the hierarchy of the Orange Order that let the people down terribly," he said.
The province's minority Catholic community see the parades as intimidating and triumphalist when they pass through nationalist enclaves.

But for the spectators in central Belfast, who had armed themselves with cans of beer and bottles of harder liquor, the 12th is an opportunity for a "good craic" (bit of fun) and more than a few drinks.
One father beside the route in Belfast stopped drinking from his can of lager just long enough to give a sip to the two-year-old daughter he was carrying in his arms.

Another middle-aged woman had positioned herself by the side of the road as early as 7 a.m. The waiting went more easily once she started making inroads into the half bottle of vodka she had had the foresight to bring with her.
There were also scenes that did not accord with the usual stereotypes of the Northern Ireland split.
Three men from the Protestant Shankill stronghold helped a Catholic nun, Sister Ann from Dublin, up onto a wall to have a better look at the parade.
She was visiting Belfast "to pray for peace and see a parade".
One of the men, "Big John", said he was sorry there were not as many people as he had expected because most had cleared out for the weekend.
Despite that, he was enjoying his chat with Sister Ann "immensely".
